blocks.text: But the aljarbuo is said to devise another stratagem as well. It sometimes covers its windows—or, more accurately, its holes—with earth at the very surface, so that they cannot be seen from outside ^{(10)}. In Arabic this is called دم [damma] damma. Alcamus: دم اليربوع حجره غطاه وسواه [damma al-yarbūʿ ḥujrahu ghaṭṭāhu wa-sawwāhu], Damma aljarbuo its burrow, that is, it covered and levelled it. Hence the burrow too is called دممة [dumama] dumama. The same Alcamus: الدممة حجرة اليربوع وتراب يجمعه اليربوع ويخرجه من الحجر فيسوي به بابه [al-dumama ḥujrat al-yarbūʿ wa-turāb yajmaʿuhu al-yarbūʿ wa-yukhrijuhu min al-ḥujr fa-yusawwī bihi bābahu], Dumama, the burrow of the aljarbuo, and the earth which it gathers and digs out of its burrow, to level its entrance with it. Accordingly, just as the opening of its burrow, covered with earth, is called نافقا [nāfiqā] naphika, so, by a metaphor taken from this, نافق [nāfaqa] naphaka, a verb of the third conjugation, means to dissemble in religion, and to profess one thing with one's mouth while keeping another hidden in one's mind. And منافق [munāfiq] munaphik means hypocrite. Damir: ظاهر بيته تراب وباطنه حفر وكذلك المنافق ظاهره ايمان وباطنه كفر [ẓāhir baytihi turāb wa-bāṭinuhu ḥafr wa-kadhālika al-munāfiq ẓāhiruhu īmān wa-bāṭinuhu kufr], The exterior of its house is earth, but the interior is hollow. Likewise, the hypocrite has faith on the outside, but unbelief within. Algiahid and others: واسم المنافق لم يكن في الجاهلية لكن لمن اسر الكفر واظهر الايمان [wa-ism al-munāfiq lam yakun fī al-jāhiliyya lākin li-man asarra al-kufr wa-aẓhara al-īmān], The name munaphik did not exist in pagan times, but (is used) of one who conceals unbelief and displays faith. Albazi: تعالي اشتق له هذا الاسم من هذا الاصل وهو من نافقا اليربوع لانه لما ابطن الكفر [taʿālā ishtaqqa lahu hādhā al-ism min hādhā al-aṣl wa-huwa min nāfiqā al-yarbūʿ li-annahu lammā abṭana al-kufr] [col. 1013] واظهر الايمان [wa-aẓhara al-īmān], God Most High derived the name of the hypocrite from this root, namely from naphika, or the hole of the mouse called aljarbuo, because unbelief is within and faith outside. The Arabs say these and many other things in commenting on Azoara 73 of the Qur'an, entitled المنافقون [al-munāfiqūn], the hypocrites. In Alcamus this animal's nest is called لغز [lughz] [II, 424] logoz, as though one were to say labyrinth, because in nests of this kind the passages are winding and very intricate. Accordingly, الغاز [alghāz] algaz in Arabic means طرق تلطوي وتشكل علي مسالكها [ṭuruq talṭawī wa-tushkil ʿalā masālikihā], paths which are twisted and entangled in their course. To this kind of mouse we should refer what Synesius says about a certain commander John near the end of letter 104: Δίκην ἀρουραίου μυὸς ἐνεδεδύκει τῇ πέτρᾳ [Dikēn arouraiou myos enededykei tē petra], Like a field mouse he had hidden himself in the rock, that is, in Bombaea, a strongly fortified stronghold in the hollow of a rock. For no other field mice nest in rock, but only the aljarbuo ^{(11)}. This is proved by these words of Ibnolgiauzi: اليربوع لا يتخذ بيته الا في موضع صلب مرتفع ليسلم من سيل او حافر ثم لا يجعلة الا عند اكمة او شجرة او صخرة ليلا يضل اذا عاد اليه [al-yarbūʿ lā yattakhidh baytahu illā fī mawḍiʿ ṣulb murtafiʿ li-yaslama min sayl aw ḥāfir thumma lā yajʿalah illā ʿinda akama aw shajara aw ṣakhra li-llā yaḍilla idhā ʿāda ilayhi], Aljarbuo makes its house only in a hard (that is, rocky) and elevated place, so that it may be safe from flooding water and from the hoof (of horses). And it establishes it only among mounds, trees, or rocks, so that it may not go astray when returning to it. This happens especially to the young of this little animal. Hence the proverb in Damir: اضل من ولد اليربوع [aḍall min walad al-yarbūʿ], He goes further astray than a young aljarbuo, said of one who wanders and settles nowhere. In the same place: وفي طباعه انه اذا مشي في ارض سهلة او لينة مشي علي موخر كفه حتي لا يعرف اثر وطيه كما يفعل الارنب [wa-fī ṭibāʿihi annahu idhā mashā fī arḍ sahla aw layyina mashā ʿalā muʾakhkhar kaffihi ḥattā lā yuʿraf athar waṭʾihi kamā yafʿal al-arnab], It is also its nature, when walking on soft and tender ground, to stand on the tips of its feet, so that its tracks may not be recognized in the places where it has trodden: this is also the hare's habit. Likewise: وهو [wa-huwa] [II, 425] يجتر ويبعر وله كرش واسنان واضراس من الفك الاعلي والاسفلي [yajtarr wa-yabʿar wa-lahu karish wa-asnān wa-aḍrās min al-fakk al-aʿlā wa-al-asfal], It also ruminates, and voids dung, and has a paunch (like ruminants), although it has teeth and molars in both the upper and the lower jaw. Another distinctive feature of this mouse is that it leaps. The Arabs express this by the particularly specific verb بحظل [baḥẓala] bachdala. Alcamus: بحظل قفز قفزان اليربوع [baḥẓala qafaza qafazān al-yarbūʿ], Bachdala, it leapt with the leap of an aljarbuo. So too Giauhari. Theophrastus observed this very thing above concerning those mice which walk on two feet: Ὅταν δὲ διώκωνται, πηδῶσι· [Hotan de diōkōntai, pēdōsi;] If anyone pursues them, they leap. In its burrows nests a kind of snake which the Arabs call جنادع [janādiʿ] gianadio, or جنادب [janādib] gianadibo. Alcamus: الجنادع الاجناش اوجنادب تكون في حجرة اليرابيع [al-janādiʿ al-ajnāsh aw janādib takūn fī ḥujrat al-yarābīʿ], Algianadio, a (kind) of snakes, or [col. 1014] gianadibo: these are in the nest of the aljarabii, which is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. If the aljarbuo mates with an ordinary mouse, the hybrid mouse born from this is called فرنب [farnab] pharnab, or phirnib. Alcamus: الفرنب الفارة او ولدها من اليربوع [al-farnab al-fāra aw waladuhā min al-yarbūʿ], Alpharnab (or alphirnib), a mouse, or its offspring by an aljarbuo. Another peculiarity of the aljarbuo is that it is eaten by the Arabs, although eating mice is otherwise forbidden to them. Damir, in the chapter الفار [al-fār] alphar, that is, On the Mouse: يحرم اكل جميع انواع الفار الا اليربوع [yaḥrum akl jamīʿ anwāʿ al-fār illā al-yarbūʿ], Eating all species of mouse is forbidden, except the aljarbuo. There is, however, some disagreement among the Arabs about this. For according to Abuchanipha: لا يوكل لانه من الحشرات [lā yuʾkal li-annahu min al-ḥasharāt], It is not eaten (the aljarbuo), because it is one of the subterranean animals. And Algazali, in the book entitled الوسيط [al-wasīṭ], The Mediator, denies that anything should be eaten من الحشرات الا الضب [min al-ḥasharāt illā al-ḍabb], of the subterranean animals except the land crocodile. Yet others also make exceptions for اليربوع وابن عرس وام حبين والقنفد والدلدل [al-yarbūʿ wa-ibn ʿirs wa-umm ḥubayn wa-al-qunfud wa-al-duldul], aljarbuo, and the weasel, and the chameleon, and the hedgehog, and the porcupine. Hence Damir says of the aljarbuo: يحل اكله لان العرب تستطيبه وتحله [yaḥill akluhu li-anna al-ʿarab tastaṭībuhu wa-tuḥilluhu], Eating it is permitted, because the Arabs allow it and enjoy it. Such, indeed, is the ruling of the great Arab canonists, Ata, Achmed Ben-Hantal, Ibnolmandsar, Abutsaur, etc. Accordingly, not only the aljarbuo but also its burrow is purchased—that is, the right to probe and search it, so that this animal may be caught in it. Yet because this generally has little success, it has become proverbial among the Arabs, as when they say: كالمشتري القاصعا باليربوع [ka-al-mushtarī al-qāṣiʿā bi-al-yarbūʿ], Like one who, for an [II, 426] aljarbuo, buys its hole. This proverb يضرب الذي يدع العين ويتبع الاثر [yuḍrab alladhī yadaʿ al-ʿayn wa-yattabiʿ al-athar], strikes at one who abandons the source and follows only the trace. In Greek one might say, Σκιὰν ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος [Skian anti tou sōmatos], A shadow instead of the body. Here too the Arabs have refined tastes, and prefer the Supharian to the other mice of this kind. Alcamus describes it thus: يربوع شفاري ضخم الاذنين وطويلهما العاري البراثين ولا يلحق سريعا والطويل والغوايم الرخو اللحم الدسم [yarbūʿ shafārī ḍakhm al-udhunayn wa-ṭawīluhumā al-ʿārī al-barāthīn wa-lā yalḥaq sarīʿan wa-al-ṭawīl wa-al-ghawāyim al-rikhw al-laḥm al-dasim], The Supharian jarbuo has thick and long ears, is without claws, so that it does not readily grasp, has long feet, and tender and fatty flesh. In Abenbitar: يربوع الاسراييلي لحم اليربوع يقد وغذا كثير ويلين البطن [yarbūʿ al-isrāyīlī laḥm al-yarbūʿ yuqadd wa-ghidhā kathīr wa-yulayyīn al-baṭn], The flesh of the aljarbuo which is dried is called Iarbuo Israëliticus. It is highly nourishing and loosens the bowels. To dry in Arabic is قد [qadda] kadda, which properly [col. 1015] means to expose meat, cut lengthwise, to the wind, as we expose it to smoke, so that the moisture may be removed. Hence قداد [qadād] kedad is used both of the hedgehog and of the aljarbuo, because both animals are dried in this way. Alcamus: القداد القنفد واليربوع [al-qadād al-qunfud wa-al-yarbūʿ], Alkedado, the hedgehog and Aljarbuo. In the Arabic versions of the sacred text the word aljarbuo occurs only once, namely Es. LXVI, 17., where the Arabic translator has: الذين ياكلون لحم الخنازير والرذالات واليربوع [alladhīna yaʾkulūna laḥm al-khanāzīr wa-al-radhālāt wa-al-yarbūʿ], Those who eat pork, and abominations, and Aljarbua, that is, the species for the genus. For the Hebrew has והעכבר, and the mouse. But the Arabic translator had reason to render it اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbua. For we have already shown that, of the whole mouse genus, this alone is eaten among the Arabs. Moreover, although עכבר achbar signifies mouse in general among the Hebrews, in Arabic this very word عكبر [ʿakbar] achbar, in the plural عكابر [ʿakābir] achabiro, signifies the male of the اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Alcamus: العكابر ذكور من اليرابيع [al-ʿakābir dhukūr min al-yarābīʿ], Alachabiro, male Aljarabii: which we have already said is the plural of the word اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo. Thus, while اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] is the name of the species, العكبر [al-ʿakbar] alachbar signifies the male, just as العطيوطة [al-ʿaṭyūṭa] alatiuta signifies the female. Alcamus: العطيوطة اليربوع الانثي [al-ʿaṭyūṭa al-yarbūʿ al-unthā], Alatiuta, the female Aljarbuo. The Portuguese Teixeira calls them ratones del mato, that is, mice of the thicket, and describes them in these words in chapter 4 of his Indian Itinerary: Son estos ratones del grandor de los grandes nuestros communes, tienen el pelo pardo tirante à blanco. Tienen de raton las orejas, manos, y la cola: cuya punta, y los ojos, y cabeça, son de conejo; y las piernas como de gazela. Corren mucho saltando, hazen cueua como conejo. Y ay dellos grande quantidad [II, 427] por aquel de sierto. Los Arabes los comen, y dizen, que son muy buenos. That is, These mice are equal in size to the largest ordinary mice, and are greyish-white in colour. They have the ears, forefeet, and tail of a mouse; the tip of the latter, their eyes, and their head are those of a rabbit; and their haunches (that is, hind legs) are those of a gazelle. They mostly run by leaping, and make burrows as rabbits do. There are very many of them in that desert (in the part of Arabia adjoining Babylonia). The Arabs use them for food, and assert that they taste excellent. These words describe the aljarbuo exactly, as everyone will acknowledge. Of the same animal Olearius writes as follows in book 6 of his Persian Itinerary, page 64: Near Terkin (in Circassia) we saw a kind of field mouse called IERBUA in Arabic. It is the size of a squirrel, and not unlike it in shape; its fur, however, is darker, and it has the head of a mouse, long ears, short forelegs, and longer hind legs. Consequently, they run only when going uphill; on level ground they generally crawl, or rise five or six feet above the ground in a leap. The tail is long and rests on the back, bare along its shaft, hairy and whitish at the tip. It was a pleasing sight to see many leaping upwards with the same impulse. They say that Babylonia and Arabia swarm with them, and that the inhabitants use them for food. Some move from the fields into houses and steal money.
